newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to meet CEOs on climate change.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to meet CEOs on climate change.

text.p: President Bill Clinton is set to meet about a dozen U.S. business leaders Monday to discuss climate change policy, White House and industry officials said.

The White House invited chief executives from oil, gas, utility, steel, chemical, and manufacturing companies, including the heads of British Petroleum Co Plc, Enron, Bethlehem Steel, and DuPont Co, according to industry sources.
"Many of these CEO's have spoken out publicly on this issue in the past," said Paul Risley, a spokesman for the White House's task force on climate change.

Industry groups and lawmakers have been pressing the Clinton administration to reveal key details of its policy for international negotiations on a climate change treaty due to be signed in Kyoto, Japan in December.

Companies that depend on cheap energy or produce oil, coal and natural gas fear that the administration will sign a treaty setting binding targets for industrialized countries to curb their carbon emissions, largely from the burning of fossil fuels, to help stem global warming.
While the administration has said it will back an agreement that sets "achievable" limits on greenhouse gases, it has not said what deadlines and specific targets it would seek in the treaty.

Under pressure from industry groups, the Senate 10 days ago passed a resolution urging the administration to reject any treaty that did not commit developing countries to cutting their greenhouse gas emissions.
Companies fear that they will be at a competitive disadvantage if only industrialized countries have to control their pollution.

Departing from most other oil companies, which argue that there is too much uncertainty about global warming to warrant taking drastic action to cut greenhouse gas emissions, BP chief executive John Browne said in a speech last May that global warming must be "taken seriously."

"To be absolutely clear, we must now focus on what can and what should be done, not because we can be certain climate change is happening, but because the possibility can't be ignored," said Browne, who will be attending the White House meeting.
